title: Lyrica and Alcohol: Is It Safe? Pregabalin Risks and Timing
excerpt: Can you drink on Lyrica? How pregabalin and alcohol stack up in your brain, the FDA breathing warning, why timing doesn't help, and the emergency signs to know.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Lyrica? How pregabalin and alcohol interact, why the dizziness and sedation stack, the FDA breathing warning, and when to call 911.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Lyrica (pregabalin) and alcohol both slow down your brain and nervous system, and together their effects stack. The most common result is stronger drowsiness, dizziness, and unsteadiness than either one causes alone, which raises the risk of falls, accidents, and poor judgment. In less common but serious cases, especially when other sedating medicines are involved, the combination can slow your breathing. The Lyrica prescribing information tells doctors to advise patients to avoid alcohol while taking it. So the one clear message of this page is simple: **don't drink on Lyrica unless your prescriber has told you it's okay for your situation**, and let them, not a website, set any limits.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink on pregabalin without your prescriber's okay. Never combine pregabalin and alcohol with opioids, benzodiazepines (like Xanax or Valium), sleeping pills, or sedating antihistamines. Don't drive or do anything risky after mixing them. Don't skip or stop your Lyrica to "make room" for a night out, because stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms and, if you take it for seizures, can trigger seizures. And if someone who has mixed them is very hard to wake, is breathing slowly or shallowly, or has blue or gray lips, call 911.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains how pregabalin and alcohol interact and what the official guidance says. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your dose, your other medicines, and your health history. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking if** you take Lyrica, Lyrica CR, or generic pregabalin, especially if you also take an opioid, an anxiety or sleep medicine, a muscle relaxer, or an antihistamine, or if you have lung disease, sleep apnea, kidney disease, or are over 65. **Call 911 right away if** someone who has taken pregabalin and alcohol is extremely sleepy or can't be woken, is confused, has slow, shallow, or noisy breathing, or has bluish lips or fingertips. For questions about a possible overdose, US readers can call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222**.

## What Lyrica Is and What It's Prescribed For

Lyrica is the brand name for **pregabalin**, a prescription medicine made by Pfizer and now widely available as a generic. There's also **Lyrica CR**, an extended-release tablet taken once a day. In the United States, pregabalin is approved for:

- **Nerve pain from diabetes** (diabetic peripheral neuropathy)
- **Nerve pain after shingles** (postherpetic neuralgia)
- **Fibromyalgia**
- **Nerve pain linked to spinal cord injury**
- **Partial-onset seizures**, as an add-on to other seizure medicines

In the UK, Europe, and some other countries, pregabalin is also approved for **generalized anxiety disorder**. Doctors sometimes prescribe it "off-label," meaning for uses outside the official approvals, for other kinds of chronic pain or anxiety.

Pregabalin belongs to a small drug family called **gabapentinoids**. Its close cousin is gabapentin (Neurontin). The two work in a very similar way, and most of what's true about mixing gabapentin with alcohol is also true for pregabalin. If you want the side-by-side, our guide to [gabapentin and alcohol](/never-hungover/gabapentin-and-alcohol) covers the sister drug in detail.

In the US, pregabalin is a **Schedule V controlled substance**, the lowest category, because it has some potential for misuse. In the UK, both pregabalin and gabapentin were reclassified as controlled drugs in 2019 for the same reason. That classification is part of why the alcohol warning is taken seriously: the drug's calming, sedating effects are exactly the ones that alcohol amplifies.

## How Pregabalin and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

To understand why the combination hits harder, it helps to know what each one does in the brain.

### What pregabalin does

Pregabalin attaches to a part of certain calcium channels on nerve cells, called the **alpha-2-delta subunit**. Calcium channels act a bit like gates that help nerve cells release their chemical messages. By binding to this part of the gate, pregabalin turns down the release of several "excitatory" messengers, the chemicals that make nerves fire. Over-active nerves are behind nerve pain and some seizures, so quieting them helps.

The trade-off is that this quieting doesn't only happen where you want it. It also slows things down more generally, which is why the two most common side effects of Lyrica are **dizziness** and **sleepiness**. Blurred vision, trouble concentrating, and feeling unsteady on your feet are also common, particularly when you first start the medicine or after a dose increase.

One detail that surprises people: despite its name, pregabalin does not act directly on the brain's GABA receptors, even though it was designed to resemble the calming messenger GABA. Its main action is on those calcium channels.

### What alcohol does

Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant. It boosts the brain's main calming system (GABA-A receptors) and dampens its main excitatory system (glutamate). The result is the familiar slowing: relaxed at first, then slower reactions, poorer coordination, slurred speech, and drowsiness as the amount rises.

### Why they add up

Pregabalin and alcohol reach the same end point, a slower brain, through different doors. When you take them together, you get both effects at once. This is called an **additive** or **pharmacodynamic** interaction, which simply means the drugs combine their effects on your body rather than changing how each other is processed.

That last point matters. The Lyrica prescribing information reports that in studies where pregabalin was given together with alcohol, there was **no change in how the body handled either drug**. Alcohol doesn't raise your pregabalin blood levels, and pregabalin doesn't change your blood alcohol level. But the same label notes that taking them together produced **additive effects on thinking and physical coordination**. In everyday terms: your blood test might look normal, but your balance, reaction time, and judgment can be noticeably worse than you'd expect from the number of drinks you've had.

### How your body clears pregabalin

Unlike many medicines, pregabalin is barely processed by the liver. The large majority of each dose leaves the body unchanged through the kidneys. Its half-life (the time it takes for the amount in your blood to fall by half) is about six hours in people with normal kidney function. A few practical consequences follow:

- **There's no liver-enzyme clash with alcohol**, which is good news for the liver but doesn't make the sedation risk any smaller.
- **People with reduced kidney function clear pregabalin more slowly**, so it can build up and hit harder. Doctors adjust the dose for this, and it's one reason kidney disease puts you in a higher-caution group.
- **If you take it every day, it's always on board.** Most people take pregabalin two or three times a day (or once a day for the CR version), so there's no time of day when you can drink with a "clear" system.

## What the Official Guidance Says

This is one of those areas where the official sources line up clearly.

**The Lyrica label.** The US prescribing information for Lyrica tells prescribers to advise patients to avoid alcohol while taking it, because pregabalin may add to the impairment of motor skills and the sedating effects of alcohol. The label also warns that dizziness and sleepiness can affect your ability to drive or operate machinery, and that patients shouldn't do these things until they know how the drug affects them.

**The FDA breathing warning.** In December 2019, the FDA warned that gabapentin and pregabalin can cause serious breathing difficulties in people who have respiratory risk factors. The FDA named the main risk factors as using these drugs together with **opioids or other medicines that depress the central nervous system**, having **lung conditions such as COPD**, and being **older**. The agency required new warnings about breathing problems on the labels of both drugs. Alcohol is itself a central nervous system depressant, so it belongs in the same category of things that raise the stakes.

**The misuse signal.** Health agencies in several countries have flagged pregabalin misuse, often in combination with opioids or alcohol, as a growing concern, and that concern is part of why pregabalin is a controlled drug. Most people who take Lyrica take it exactly as prescribed, but it explains why prescribers ask about alcohol and other sedatives before starting it.

Put together, the guidance says: **alcohol makes pregabalin's main side effects stronger, the combination is especially risky with other sedatives or breathing problems, and the decision about whether any drinking is safe for you belongs to your prescriber.**

## What It Actually Feels Like to Mix Them

People describe the combination in fairly consistent ways, and knowing the pattern can help you recognize when things are going wrong.

**Common effects:**

- **Feeling drunk faster** than usual, or more drunk than the number of drinks would explain
- **Strong dizziness** or a spinning, light-headed feeling, especially when standing up
- **Heavy drowsiness**, sometimes falling asleep unexpectedly
- **Poor balance and clumsiness**, with a higher chance of tripping or falling
- **Blurred or double vision**
- **Trouble thinking clearly**, slowed speech, or memory gaps for parts of the evening

**Serious effects that need emergency help:**

- Being very hard to wake, or not waking at all
- Slow, shallow, irregular, or noisy breathing, including heavy snoring or gurgling in someone you can't rouse
- Blue or gray lips or fingertips
- Severe confusion or not responding normally
- Vomiting while very drowsy (a choking risk)

If you see any of the serious signs, **call 911**. While you wait, keep the person on their side so they don't choke if they vomit, and stay with them. Don't let them "sleep it off" alone.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

Some people should treat any drinking on pregabalin as something to clear with their doctor first, and many will be told not to drink at all:

- **Anyone also taking opioids**, including prescription painkillers like oxycodone, hydrocodone, or tramadol. This is the combination the FDA was most concerned about. Our pages on [tramadol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tramadol-and-alcohol) and the wider [alcohol and medications hub](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications) explain why stacking sedatives is so risky.
- **Anyone taking benzodiazepines or sleep medicines**, such as Xanax, Valium, Klonopin, or Ambien. See [Xanax and alcohol](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol) for more on that class.
- **Anyone taking muscle relaxers** or sedating antihistamines. Our guide to [muscle relaxers and alcohol](/never-hungover/muscle-relaxers-and-alcohol) covers that group.
- **People over 65.** Older adults are more sensitive to sedation and dizziness and more likely to be hurt in a fall. The FDA named older age as a breathing risk factor.
- **People with COPD, asthma, sleep apnea, or other breathing conditions.**
- **People with kidney disease**, who clear pregabalin more slowly.
- **People who take pregabalin for seizures**, because heavy drinking, hangovers, and disrupted sleep can all make seizures more likely.
- **People who drive for work, operate machinery, or care for young children.**

## Timing: Is There a Safe Gap Between a Dose and a Drink?

This is one of the most searched questions, and the honest answer is that **there's no official waiting period that applies to everyone**. Anyone who gives you an exact number of hours is guessing.

Here's what is true:

- **If you take pregabalin regularly, it's in your system all the time.** Most people are on a schedule of two or three doses a day, which is designed to keep a steady level in the blood. Spacing a drink away from a pill doesn't really get you out from under the effect.
- **The effect peaks soon after a dose.** Pregabalin is absorbed quickly, with blood levels typically peaking within about an hour and a half of a dose. Drinking around that time is likely to hit hardest.
- **Clearing the drug fully takes days, not hours.** With a half-life of about six hours, it takes roughly a day or more for most of the drug to leave after your last dose, and longer if your kidneys are slower.
- **Don't skip or stop doses to drink.** This is important enough to have its own section below.

If you only take pregabalin occasionally, "as needed," ask your prescriber how they want you to handle alcohol. That's a question with a personal answer, and it's a quick one for them to give.

## Don't Stop Your Lyrica to Make Room for Drinking

It can be tempting to skip a dose or stop for a few days before a wedding or a holiday so you can drink. Please don't do this without talking to your prescriber.

The Lyrica label warns against stopping suddenly. When pregabalin is stopped abruptly, people have reported **trouble sleeping, nausea, headache, anxiety, sweating, and diarrhea**, and the label advises tapering off gradually over at least a week. If you take it for seizures, stopping suddenly can bring on seizures. Your original pain or anxiety can also come roaring back.

There's also a cruel overlap here. Those withdrawal symptoms, the poor sleep, the nausea, the headache, the anxiety, look a lot like a hangover. Mixing a sudden stop with a night of drinking can leave you feeling much worse than either alone, and it can be hard to tell which is causing what.

If an upcoming event matters to you, tell your prescriber. They may have a plan that keeps you safe, or they may simply tell you that skipping alcohol that night is the better option. Either way, you'll know.

## Lyrica, Alcohol, and the Morning After

Even when the night goes fine, the combination can shape the next day.

- **Grogginess can carry over.** Pregabalin's sleepiness plus the poor-quality sleep alcohol causes can make the next morning slower than a usual hangover. Be careful about driving early the next day.
- **Dizziness can linger.** Both pregabalin and a hangover can leave you light-headed, especially when you stand up quickly. Get up slowly and drink water.
- **Be careful what you take for the hangover.** Don't reach for a sedating "PM" product, a sleep aid, or an antihistamine to help you rest after drinking on pregabalin. Those add another layer of sedation. Our guide to [sleep aids and alcohol](/never-hungover/sleep-aids-and-alcohol) explains why.
- **Don't double up your next dose** if you missed one the night before. Take your medicine as prescribed, and if you're unsure what to do about a missed dose, ask a pharmacist.

## Weight Gain, Swelling, and Other Side Effects That Alcohol Can Worsen

Beyond sedation, pregabalin has a few other well-known side effects that are worth knowing about if you drink:

- **Weight gain and fluid retention (swelling).** Pregabalin can cause weight gain and swelling in the hands, feet, or ankles. Alcohol adds calories and can affect fluid balance, so regular drinking can make these harder to manage.
- **Blurred vision.** Pregabalin can blur vision, and alcohol does too. Together, they make driving and night-time walking riskier.
- **Mood changes.** Like all seizure medicines, pregabalin carries a label warning about rare suicidal thoughts or behavior. Alcohol can lower mood, especially the day after. If you notice new or worsening depression, anxiety, or thoughts of self-harm, contact your doctor right away. In the US, you can call or text **988** for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

None of this is a reason to panic about your medicine. It's a reason to keep your prescriber in the loop about how much you drink, so they can factor it in.

## How to Talk to Your Prescriber About Drinking

Some people avoid this conversation because they're worried about being judged. Prescribers ask about alcohol because it genuinely changes how safe a medicine is, and it's one of the most common questions they get. A few ways to make the conversation easy:

- **Be specific and honest.** "I usually have two glasses of wine on Friday and Saturday" is far more useful than "I drink socially."
- **Ask the direct question.** "Is it safe for me to have any alcohol on my current dose? If so, how much?"
- **Bring up your full medication list**, including over-the-counter sleep aids, antihistamines, and supplements.
- **Ask about special events.** "I have a wedding next month. What do you recommend?"
- **Ask what to do if you've already mixed them** and felt unwell, so you know your warning signs.

If your prescriber gives you the okay for occasional, light drinking, follow the limits they set. Until then, the safe default is no alcohol.

## A Note on Drinking Patterns

This article is written for people who take pregabalin for pain, nerve symptoms, seizures, or anxiety and want to know whether they can have a drink. It isn't a guide to drinking less in general. If you notice that you keep searching for ways to drink while on a medicine that warns against it, that's a useful thing to mention to your doctor. It's a common, normal conversation, and they'd rather know.

## What About DHM and Other Hangover Supplements?

People who take pregabalin sometimes ask whether a hangover supplement like DHM (dihydromyricetin) is safe to use with it. The honest answer is that nobody has studied DHM together with pregabalin in people, so there is no good evidence either way about how they interact.

What we do know: pregabalin is cleared mostly by the kidneys rather than by the liver enzymes that process many drugs, so a classic liver-enzyme interaction seems less likely. But DHM's best-studied effect, mostly in animal research, involves the brain's GABA-A receptors, the same calming system alcohol acts on. Anything that works on the brain's calming systems is worth clearing with your prescriber before you combine it with a sedating medicine. And no supplement makes it safe to drink on Lyrica, reduces the dizziness and sedation of the combination, or protects your breathing.

If your prescriber is comfortable with you using DHM, think of it as a modest helper for occasional social drinking, not a safety net. Popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what is and isn't known about DHM alongside common medicines, our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains typical amounts and timing, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. For general habits that make any night of drinking easier on your body, see [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## The Bottom Line

- Lyrica (pregabalin) and alcohol both slow the brain, and together the effects add up: more dizziness, more sleepiness, worse coordination, and a higher risk of falls and accidents.
- Alcohol doesn't change your pregabalin blood levels, but it does make you more impaired than you'd expect. That's the trap.
- The Lyrica label tells prescribers to advise patients to avoid alcohol, and the FDA has warned about breathing problems when gabapentinoids are combined with other sedatives, in older adults, and in people with lung disease.
- **Talk to your prescriber before drinking.** Any limit should come from them, based on your dose, your kidneys, your age, and your other medicines.
- Never mix pregabalin and alcohol with opioids, benzodiazepines, sleeping pills, or sedating antihistamines, and never drive after combining them.
- Don't stop or skip your Lyrica to drink. Stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms and seizures.
- If someone is very hard to wake, breathing slowly, or has blue lips, call 911.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Lyrica?**

The Lyrica prescribing information tells doctors to advise patients to avoid alcohol, because pregabalin can add to alcohol's sedating effects and its impact on coordination. Whether any drinking is acceptable for you depends on your dose, your kidney function, your age, and your other medicines, so ask your prescriber before you drink. If they haven't said it's okay, the safe default is no alcohol.

**What happens if you mix pregabalin and alcohol?**

The two effects stack. Most people notice stronger dizziness, sleepiness, unsteadiness, blurred vision, and slower thinking than either causes alone, which raises the risk of falls and accidents. Alcohol doesn't change your pregabalin blood levels, but you can be more impaired than you'd expect. With opioids, other sedatives, lung disease, or older age, the combination can also slow breathing, which is an emergency.

**How long after taking Lyrica can I drink?**

There's no official waiting period that applies to everyone. If you take pregabalin on a regular schedule, it's in your system all the time, so spacing a drink away from a pill doesn't remove the effect. The effect is strongest in the first couple of hours after a dose. Ask your prescriber how they want you to handle alcohol, and never skip doses to make room for drinking.

**Can I skip my Lyrica dose so I can drink?**

Don't do this without talking to your prescriber. Stopping pregabalin suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms such as trouble sleeping, nausea, headache, anxiety, sweating, and diarrhea, and if you take it for seizures, stopping abruptly can trigger seizures. The label advises tapering off over at least a week when stopping.

**Is pregabalin and alcohol the same risk as gabapentin and alcohol?**

Very similar. Pregabalin and gabapentin belong to the same drug family and work in the same way, and both carry the same type of warning about sedation and the 2019 FDA warning about breathing problems with other sedatives. Pregabalin is absorbed more quickly and predictably, but the safety message is the same: talk to your prescriber before drinking on either one.

**What are the emergency signs after mixing Lyrica and alcohol?**

Call 911 if someone is very hard to wake or won't wake up, has slow, shallow, irregular, or noisy breathing, has blue or gray lips or fingertips, is severely confused, or is vomiting while very drowsy. Keep them on their side and stay with them until help arrives. Don't let them sleep it off alone.

**Does DHM make it safe to drink on Lyrica?**

No. There's no good evidence that DHM reduces the dizziness, sedation, or breathing risk of combining pregabalin and alcohol, and DHM hasn't been studied alongside pregabalin in people. Because DHM's best-studied effects involve the brain's calming system, ask your prescriber before using it with a sedating medicine.
